text: The Montana race is just one piece of the Senate puzzle in the upcoming elections. Both parties are dealing with surprises in some races. And recent polls are reshaping and redefining others.

Republicans want to protect their 55-seat majority, but for Democrats to seize control, they must win almost every competitive Senate seat this fall and avoid losing any now held by Democrats. That's a tall order.
For some analysis, we turn to Jennifer Duffy. She's the editor of the Cook Political Report. She joins us here in our studios. Jennifer, so glad you're here.
Thanks for having me.
Give us, if you could, to start this off, the lay of the land.

The lay of the land is this focus on the six seats Democrats need to take the majority. Today, I think there are six Senate races out there that are too close to call that are held by Republicans. By contrast, Democrats only have one seat that they are in real danger of losing.

You know, it's not hard for me to see how Democrats get three seats, four seats, five seats. That sixth seat will be a little harder. They need almost everything to go right for them on election night.
Tick through the six seats for us.

Conrad Burns in Montana. That's what we just heard. Rick Santorum of Pennsylvania, Mike Dewine in Ohio, Lincoln Chafee in Rhode Island, Jim Talent in Missouri and then the open seat in Tennessee, where Bill Frist is retiring.
For Democrats, their one real endangered seat, believe it or not, is in the very blue state of New Jersey.
Bob Menendez is now under investigation, running against a candidate with a quite familiar name in that region.

That's right. You know, Menendez was appointed to the Senate in December by Jon Corzine, who won the governor's race. Tom Kean, Jr. is the Republican. He's a state senator obviously. His father was a very, very popular governor. His most recent position was co-chair of the 9/11 Commission.

Now, the Kean name carries a great deal of cache. And Menendez, as you noted, has some of his own problems. Not only is he under investigation, but scandal seems to be kicking up in other places around the state.
That's what I wondered. I wondered if voters there might be feeling a bit of scandal fatigue. The former governor, Jim McGreevy, is out right now hawking his book.

That's right. There was a state senator who pleaded guilty a couple of weeks ago to corruption. There are rumors of more indictments. Even in New Jersey, they might hit scandal fatigue. But I have to tell you, New Jersey's very blue state and Republicans have struggled there in good political environments for them. This is not a good environment.
But looking at the data, you know, consistently over the last three or four months, Tom Kean is more than holding his own here.

Let's go to Tennessee now. Open seat to succeed retiring Senate Majority Leader Bill Frist. Democratic Congressman Harold Ford running against Republican Bob Corker. Now Corker came out of the primaries in a comfort zone. All that has changed in the last eight weeks. This is a case where Corker's past seems to have caught up with him. A controversy over his handling of the 911 system when he was mayor of Chattanooga. Is that correct?

MS. DUFFY: That is correct. He comes right out of the primary and there were two stories that appeared right away. One had to do with his business as a developer and whether or not they essentially paved over environmentally sensitive land to build an access road for a Wal-Mart.

The second was this 911 controversy where many calls didn't get answered. Meanwhile, I think a lot of people ignored the work that Congressman Ford has been doing for the last 14, 15 months. Traveling the state, he's inoculated himself as best he can against two issues that he will face in this race.
Those two issues being?

MS. DUFFY: The first is that if Harold Ford is elected to the Senate, he will be the first African American from a Southern state to go to the Senate since Reconstruction. The second is his rather notorious family. You know, his father held the House seat he now sits in, he's had uncles who have served in the state legislature, and one of them faces trial on corruption charges early next year.
Ford has tried very hard to deal with this issue. He essentially says, you know, nothing's going to make me stop loving my family. But if they did something wrong, they need to pay the price.
Now easy to understand why the family baggage would be an issue but why would his position as the first black senator from the South be an issue, an impediment?

MS. DUFFY: Well, here we are in 2006 and that no southern state has sent an African-American to the Senate I think tells us that it's still very hard to get elected as an African-American there. One of the things that helps Ford is that his record is more moderate than most Democrats in the House.
Jennifer, thanks so much.
MS. DUFFY: Thank you.
Jennifer Duffy, she's the editor of The Cook Political Report.
7-Eleven drops longtime partner Citgo. That story, and Bob Mondello's review of the new film, The Last King of Scotland, just ahead on ALL THINGS CONSIDERED.
From NPR News, this is ALL THINGS CONSIDERED. I'm Robert Siegel.

Now, the nationwide race for control of the Congress. Based on polls, it is now considered possible that the Democrats could take control of the House of Representatives. And control of the U.S. Senate, which seems almost certain to remain in Republican hands just a few months ago, now appears to be the subject of a real contest.
Joining us to talk about this are Jennifer Duffy, who is the Senate expert for The Cook Political Report. Welcome back to the program, Jennifer Duffy.
(The Cook Political Report): Thank you.
And Chuck Todd, who's editor in chief of the online political digest Hotline. Welcomes to the program, Chuck Todd.

speaker_label: Mr. CHUCK TODD (Online Political Digest, Hotline)
text: Great. Thank you.
Firs the House, Chuck. What is the informed view nowadays of how close the race is for a majority of the House of Representatives in November?

speaker_label: Mr. CHUCK TODD (Online Political Digest, Hotline)
text: It seems like there's been a mindset shift, particularly inside the Beltway, but now you're sort of seeing it seep outside the Beltway, where among the smart strategists, particularly in the Republican side, there's total doom and gloom with the Republicans that they can keep control of the House. In fact, it's almost a given, they think, that they lose the House. The question is how badly, what kind of deficit will they have going into '08 - sort of.

speaker_label: Mr. CHUCK TODD (Online Political Digest, Hotline)
text: But that said, you know, they are still fighting this thing, like maybe they can keep their losses to 10 or 12 seats. You know, the Democrats need 15 to gain control, and ever since the Mark Foley scandal, it seems like they've continued to sort of - the Republicans are giving away seats. They've given away a seat with Tom DeLay, they've given away a seat in Arizona. Now it appears they've given away one in Florida. They've given away one, potentially, in Ohio. Then you have the news about the national party potentially pulling out of Ohio for a Senate race.

speaker_label: Mr. CHUCK TODD (Online Political Digest, Hotline)
text: Well, that has a trickle down effect on four other House races in that state. So suddenly getting to 15 seats doesn't seem very difficult. The question is can Republicans keep the Democrats from winning, say, more than 20 seats. And I think it appears that they're almost in that mode as opposed to the mode of just trying to keep control. It's getting very difficult.

I just want you to pursue your geographical division of America into inside the Beltway, that is in and around Washington, D.C., and the rest of the country. Were state political operatives any more sensitive to this? Were they aware of what was going on?

speaker_label: Mr. CHUCK TODD (Online Political Digest, Hotline)
text: Well, I think what's happening is this pessimism is contagious. In fact, the genius of this Republican Party for so long is that they always avoided pessimism. You know, pessimism was for the Democratic Party mindset. They were always pessimistic, they always were doubting their ability to win. They always would snatch defeat from victory, where the Republicans always had this ability to be optimistic even in times when they shouldn't have been, and yet they were able to pull victory from defeat.

speaker_label: Mr. CHUCK TODD (Online Political Digest, Hotline)
text: And so this time, boy, you're just not seeing it. We're seeing all sorts of evidence in various states where you just have Republican volunteers sort of in a doom and gloom mode wondering boy, if our folks back in Washington don't think we can win, then why should I make my 100 phone calls tonight? Why should I do my door knocking? And so that's the danger here the Republican Party faces, not just in the House races, but then that can trickle up into Senate races and governors' races.

Well Jennifer Duffy, as we heard from Chuck Todd, there is a story that the New York Times put on the front page today, but it's been around before that, that the Republicans are no longer sending national money to support the campaign of Republican incumbent Senator Mike DeWine in Ohio. What's the significance of that?

Well, I think the significance is that in some ways, the parties raised a white flag in Ohio. The environment in Ohio has been bad for Republicans all cycle. I think the latest downturn in Republican numbers nationally has mad it worse. It's almost a hit that these Republican candidates in Ohio can't sustain now. You know, Senator DeWine certainly has a sizable war chest. He is going to continue his campaign, it just won't be with a lot of help from the Republican Party. What it does tell us, though, is that they are now shifting what they're calling their firewall to seats they need to maintain in order to maintain their majority.
And that would include which Senate seats?
Well, there are three of them right now. You're looking at Missouri, Tennessee and Virginia. If Democrats want control, they need to win two or three of those seats.

In the House races, as we heard from Chuck Todd, the Mark Foley -Congressman Mark Foley - scandal seems to have had some impact. Do voters make any distinction when it comes to the Senate, or what do you get a sense is driving so many voters in the polls, at least, away from, well, even some Republican incumbents who seemed pretty safe earlier this year.

You know, I think the Foley scandal per se has not had a direct impact on Senate races. But if you take Mark Foley and continued bad news in Iraq and Bob Woodward's book, State of Denial, which has been quite critical of the administration, and the national security estimates - intelligence estimates - because they were all - all these things happened around the same time. It's almost like it just handed every Republican candidate 20 more pounds of wet sand to carry around.
You mean, if you've been standing by the president on Iraq all this time and being a good soldier in the GOP, suddenly it's not such an asset right now.
It's not an asset, and I just think that voters, you know, Democrats and a lot of independents are angry, and Republicans are discouraged.

There are three more weeks of campaigning, and in many states, the candidates either for senator or governor have had their big debates already. Jennifer, what does experience tell you about how much motion there might be typically in the last three weeks of a non-presidential election year? Can it be a lot?

Well, I think, you know, in these close races, certainly. What is left to do is, you know, the final attacks back and forth, trying to score some points there, and then it is getting your voters out to the polls. You know, Democrats, especially in Senate races this year, feel that they have put, you know, an operation on the ground to do that, to sort of go head to head with Republicans' very successful turnout operation over the last two elections. This is pretty much what goes on in the last three weeks.

I'm curious to hear from both of you before I let you go. Congressman Foley's problems may have dominated the news for a week or so, but does this election - is it likely to go down as the Iraq election? What do you think, Chuck Todd?

speaker_label: Mr. CHUCK TODD (Online Political Digest, Hotline)
text: Oh, I think it definitely will. All and all, look, this thing is about Iraq. It's been about Iraq for 18 months, and it's going to be, I think, about Iraq at the end of the day, particularly if the Democrats win. If the Democrats don't win, we're going to have a harder time saying that this was about Iraq.
Jennifer Duffy?

Now only is about Iraq, but as mid-term elections tend to be, this is also a referendum on President Bush and his policies on Iraq, on national security, on the economy. You know, this is what mid-term elections are about. They are referendums on the party in power.
Well, thanks to both of you for talking politics with us today. Jennifer Duffy of The Cook Political Report and Chuck Todd of the Hotline. Thanks.
Thank you.

speaker_label: Mr. CHUCK TODD (Online Political Digest, Hotline)
text: And thank you.
